subject: technology
essential_question: How does the way we represent data change what we can do with it?
standards: Michigan Computer Science: Algorithms and Programming
project_brief: Implement and measure two data structures for the same task and justify the selection with evidence. This is the grade 10 culminating project for "Data Representation and Structures" (ma-g10-technology-u01, unit 1), built around numeric text and binary encoding, arrays and lists, dictionaries and records, stacks and queues, and nested and tabular structures. Collect or use a small, fictional or already-approved data set related to numeric text and binary encoding, arrays and lists, dictionaries and records, and stacks and queues, and turn it into a labeled visual with a one-paragraph, evidence-based conclusion.
requirements: Address every topic listed for this unit: numeric text and binary encoding, arrays and lists, dictionaries and records, stacks and queues, nested and tabular structures, and choosing a structure for a problem.
Meet the performance task as written: Implement and measure two data structures for the same task and justify the selection with evidence.
Show your work or process, not just a final result — a process note, sketch log, commit history, or draft trail.
Complete the checklist in this package before submitting.
primary_task: Collect or use a small, fictional or already-approved data set related to numeric text and binary encoding, arrays and lists, dictionaries and records, and stacks and queues, and turn it into a labeled visual with a one-paragraph, evidence-based conclusion.
test_or_check_criteria: Every claim or design choice in the submission can be traced to numeric text and binary encoding or another named topic from this unit — nothing is left unexplained.
The submission runs, displays, or demonstrates correctly on at least two different sample inputs or scenarios the student chooses.
No real password, API key, account credential, precise location, or other real personal/system data appears anywhere in the submission — fictional or sandbox examples only.
The student can explain, in their own words, why each step or decision was made, not just that it works.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: This project never touches a real account, a real password or API key, a live production system, or another person's real data. Use fictional names, sandbox environments, local files, or already-approved sample data throughout. Submit code, screenshots of your own sandbox, diagrams, or a written walkthrough — a live public deployment is never required.

copyright_and_authorship: The final submitted work must remain your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI assistant may help you plan, explain a concept, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but may not produce the graded work itself. Never request, store, or submit a real password, API key, access token, or other real credential; use only fictional accounts and sandboxed or offline systems.
remediation: If the project stalls, step back to the smallest version of the task: rebuild just the part covering numeric text and binary encoding in isolation, using a worked example from this unit as a model, then re-attach it to the full project once that smaller piece works and you can explain why.
extension: Once the core project is working, extend it to handle a new constraint or edge case related to arrays and lists, or compare two different approaches to the same problem and explain the real tradeoff between them in your own words.
